cse-2021-2-cs-35.approach: Trace the two loops: count the nodes the first loop builds, then follow `head` through the second loop and check which `next` field is read before it was ever written.

steps.title: Nodes created
steps.body: One node before the loop (value 0) plus one per iteration of \`index = 1..3\`: values 1, 2, 3. So the list is $0 \to 1 \to 2 \to 3$ — **4 nodes**. The last node's \`next\` is never assigned; \`malloc\` leaves it **uninitialized** (garbage).

steps.title: Second loop
steps.body:
Each iteration prints \`head->value\`, advances \`head = head->next\`, then prints \`head->value\` again.

| index | head before | head after advance |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | node 0 | node 1 |
| 1 | node 1 | node 2 |
| 2 | node 2 | node 3 |
| 3 | node 3 | **garbage** (node 3's \`next\`) |

In the last iteration \`head->value\` dereferences that garbage pointer.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.body: Dereferencing an uninitialized pointer is undefined behaviour and may crash at run time (segmentation fault). The loop runs exactly 4 times (no infinite loop), and \`main\` without \`return\` is legal in C99 (returns 0) — at worst a warning in C89, never an error.

Both loops have fixed bounds (index runs to 3 and stops); nothing loops forever.
Falling off the end of `main` is allowed (C99 returns 0 implicitly); compilers do not report it as an error.
In the 4th iteration `head` becomes node 3's uninitialized `next`, and `head->value` dereferences it — a possible run-time crash.

cse-2021-2-cs-43.approach: Check Coffman conditions: the scheme lets a requester forcibly take a resource from its owner, so "no preemption" is broken and deadlock cannot occur. But victims are restarted and can be preempted again and again.

steps.title: Deadlock
steps.body: A process requesting a held resource never waits: it terminates the owner, takes the resource, and restarts the owner. Since nobody waits holding resources, the circular-wait/no-preemption conditions cannot both hold — **deadlock cannot occur** (A true). Everything happens under the global lock \`L\`, and an instance still has a single owner at any time — **mutual exclusion is preserved** (D false).

steps.title: Livelock and starvation
steps.body: P1 holds $R_1$, P2 holds $R_2$. P1 requests $R_2$ → kills/restarts P2. P2 restarts, grabs $R_2$ back, requests $R_1$ → kills/restarts P1, and so on. Both keep running but neither finishes — **livelock** (B true). Likewise one unlucky process can be terminated every time it gets going while others finish — **starvation** (C true).

optionAnalysis.reason: Requests are satisfied by preempting the owner, so no process ever waits for a held resource; deadlock is prevented.
Two processes can keep terminating and restarting each other without progress.
A process can be chosen as the victim repeatedly and never complete.
Ownership changes only under the global lock, and the old owner releases everything first; at most one owner per instance at any time.

pitfalls: Confusing "preempting a resource" with "violating mutual exclusion" — the resource is handed over, never shared.
cse-2021-2-cs-43.verification: Coffman check: hold-and-wait and no-preemption are both broken (no one waits; holders are preempted), so deadlock is impossible.

Dependent EX starts right after the producer's EX. EX lengths: ADD 1, MUL 2. I1's EX is in cycle 3; then EX cycles run back-to-back:
$$\underbrace{3}_{\text{I1 EX}} + \underbrace{(2 + 1 + 2 + 1 + 2 + 1 + 2)}_{\text{I2..I8 EX cycles}} = 3 + 11 = 14 \Rightarrow \text{last EX ends in cycle } 14$$
Then MEM (15), WB (16): **16 cycles**.

Registers are read in EX, so a dependent EX can start only in the cycle after the producer's WB. Each instruction then costs its EX length + MEM + WB:
- I1: EX 3, WB 5.
- each MUL: EX 2 cycles + MEM + WB = 4 cycles after the previous WB; each ADD: 3 cycles.

$$5 + 4\cdot 4 + 3 \cdot 3 = 5 + 16 + 9 = 30 \text{ cycles}$$

steps.title: Speedup
steps.body: $$\text{Speedup} = \frac{30}{16} = 1.875 \approx 1.87\text{–}1.88$$

pitfalls: Allowing the dependent EX in the same cycle as the producer's WB — the register read is in EX, and the official key (1.87–1.88) assumes it waits.
Forgetting that MUL occupies EX for 2 cycles even with forwarding.
cse-2021-2-cs-53.verification: Built both schedules cycle by cycle (diagrams): last WB is cycle 16 with forwarding and cycle 30 without.

cse-2021-2-cs-54.approach: Compute the offered load G in frames per frame-time and use the pure ALOHA throughput $S = G e^{-2G}$ (success needs no other transmission in a 2-frame-time vulnerable window).

steps.title: Offered load
steps.body: Frame time $T = \frac{1000}{10^6} = 1$ ms. $G = 1000 \text{ frames/s} \times 10^{-3}\text{ s} = 1$ frame per frame-time.

steps.title: Throughput
steps.body:
$$S = G e^{-2G} = 1 \cdot e^{-2} \approx 0.1353 \text{ frames per frame-time}$$
$$0.1353 \times 1000 \text{ frame-times/s} \approx 135 \text{ frames/s}$$

pitfalls: Using slotted ALOHA $Ge^{-G}$ (would give 368).
Reporting 0.135 instead of frames per second.

cse-2021-2-cs-55.approach: Process vertices in topological order and keep the best (maximum) product into each vertex: $q(v) = \max_{u \to v} q(u)\cdot w(u,v)$, like longest-path DP on a DAG.

steps.title: Middle vertices
steps.body:
- $q(d) = \max(q(c)\cdot 1,\ q(a)\cdot 1) = \max(1, 9) = 9$
- $q(e) = \max(q(b)\cdot 1,\ q(d)\cdot 9) = \max(9, 81) = 81$
- $q(g) = \max(q(f)\cdot 1,\ q(d)\cdot 9) = \max(9, 81) = 81$

pitfalls: Adding weights instead of multiplying.
Taking the path through c (weight 1) to d instead of through a (weight 9).
cse-2021-2-cs-55.verification: Best path to t: s→a→d→e→t = 9·1·9·9 = 729; the alternative via g gives at most 81. Sum s,a,b,c,d,e,f,g,t = 1+9+9+1+9+81+9+81+729 = 929.
